message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge a security deposit, but it must be returned within 30 days after you move out, unless you give a written notice of intent to stay.
• The deposit can be used only for unpaid rent, damages beyond normal wear, or cleaning if the lease specifies it. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Take photos or videos of the unit when you move in and out. | | **Habitability** | • Texas law requires landlords to keep the premises in a habitable condition (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, structural safety).
• The landlord must repair any major defects that affect health or safety. | • Report problems in writing (email or letter) and keep a copy.
• If repairs are not made within a reasonable time, you may withhold rent or pursue a repair‑and‑deduct remedy (see below). | | **Repair‑and‑Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to fix a major defect, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from your rent, provided you give the landlord written notice and keep receipts. | • Document the defect, send a written notice, keep receipts, and calculate the deduction carefully. | | **Rent Increases** | • For month‑to‑month leases, landlords can raise rent at the end of each lease term or with 30 days’ written notice.
• For fixed‑term leases, rent cannot be increased during the term unless the lease allows it. | • Review your lease for any rent‑increase clauses. | | **Notice to Vacate** | • For month‑to‑month tenancy, landlords must give at least 30 days’ written notice to terminate.
• For fixed‑term leases, the lease ends automatically unless you or the landlord renews. | • Provide written notice if you plan to move out; keep a copy. | | **Privacy & Entry** | • Landlords must give at least 24 hours’ written notice before entering, except in emergencies.
• Entry is allowed for repairs, inspections, or showing the unit to prospective tenants or buyers. | • Keep a log of any entries; if you suspect unlawful entry, document it. | | **Discrimination** | • Under federal Fair Housing Act and Texas law, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, or source of income (e.g., public assistance). | • If you suspect discrimination, file a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the Texas eviction procedure: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment of rent, 30‑day notice for lease termination).
• If you fail to comply, the landlord can file an unlawful detainer action in court. | • Respond promptly to notices; if you believe the notice is improper, consult an attorney. | | **Lease Terms & Modifications** | • Any changes to the lease must be in writing and signed by both parties.
• Oral agreements are generally enforceable but harder to prove. | • Keep all lease documents and any addendums. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. If the landlord pays, they must maintain the utility service. | • Verify utility responsibilities in the lease. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • Many leases allow subletting or assignment with landlord’s consent.
• Texas law does not prohibit subletting, but the lease may restrict it. | • Obtain written permission before subletting. | | **Maintenance of Common Areas** | • Landlords must keep common areas (hallways, stairwells, laundry rooms) safe and clean. | • Report any hazards in common areas. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to use the premises without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • If the landlord interferes (e.g., frequent visits, noise), document incidents. | | **Legal Remedies** | • If the landlord violates your rights, you can:
1. File a complaint with HUD or Texas Commission on Human Rights.
2. Seek a court order (e.g., injunction, damages).
3. Withhold rent (after following repair‑and‑deduct rules). | • Keep all correspondence and receipts; consider legal counsel for serious disputes. | ### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Understand rent amount, due dates, security deposit, pet policy, maintenance responsibilities, and notice periods. 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written notices, and receipts help protect you. 3. **Know the Notice Requirements** – 24‑hour notice for entry, 30‑day notice for termination, 3‑day notice for non‑payment. 4. **Report Problems Promptly** – Send written notice to the landlord and keep copies. 5. **Keep Records of Repairs** – If you repair something yourself, keep receipts and calculate the deduction. 6. **Know Your Rights to Privacy and Quiet Enjoyment** – Landlords cannot enter without notice or interfere with your use of the unit. 7. **Seek Help if Needed** – Contact local tenant‑rights groups, HUD, or a lawyer if you face eviction, discrimination, or other violations. --- #### Resources - **Texas Property Code** – The statutory framework for landlord‑tenant relations. - **HUD – Fair Housing** – For discrimination complaints. - **Texas Commission on Human Rights** – For state‑level discrimination complaints. - **Local Tenant‑Rights Organizations** – e.g., Texas Tenants Union, local legal aid clinics. Feel free to ask if you need more detail on any specific point or if you’d like guidance on how to handle a particular situation.
